questions.question: A thread is considered a basic unit of what?
questions.explanation: A thread is the basic unit of CPU utilization, comprising a thread ID, a program counter, a register set, and a stack.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT uniquely owned by a single thread (i.e., it is shared with other threads in the process)?
questions.explanation: Each thread has its own program counter, register set, and stack, but shares the code section, data section, and OS resources with peer threads in the same process.

questions.question: Why are threads generally preferred over processes for modern applications?
options: Thread creation is lightweight compared to processes
Threads run independently on different hard drives
questions.correctAnswer: Thread creation is lightweight compared to processes
questions.explanation: Process creation is heavyweight and resource-intensive, whereas thread creation is lightweight and shares the existing process address space and resources.

questions.question: Placing multiple computing cores on a single processing chip is known as:
questions.explanation: Multicore systems place multiple computing cores on a single processor chip, where each core appears as a separate processor to the OS.

questions.question: Which multicore programming challenge ensures that tasks perform equal work of equal value?
questions.explanation: Balance ensures that the tasks divided across cores perform equal work of equal value so one core is not underutilized.

questions.question: A system that can perform more than one task simultaneously exhibits:
questions.explanation: A system is parallel if it can perform more than one task simultaneously across multiple cores.

questions.question: A single-core system with a scheduler switching between tasks provides:
questions.explanation: Concurrency supports more than one task making progress over time, which is possible on a single core by interleaving execution via scheduling.

questions.question: Which type of parallelism distributes subsets of the same data across multiple cores to perform the same operation?
questions.explanation: Data parallelism distributes subsets of the same data across multiple cores and performs the same operation on each subset.

questions.question: Threads managed without kernel support by a user-level library are called:
questions.explanation: User threads are managed above the kernel by a user-level threads library without direct kernel awareness.

questions.question: Which multithreading model maps many user-level threads to a single kernel thread?
questions.explanation: The Many-to-One model maps multiple user-level threads to one kernel thread.

questions.question: In the Many-to-One multithreading model, what happens if one user thread makes a blocking system call?
questions.explanation: Because only one kernel thread backs all user threads in the Many-to-One model, a blocking system call by any thread blocks the entire process.

questions.question: Which multithreading model maps each user-level thread directly to a kernel thread?
questions.explanation: The One-to-One model maps each user-level thread to its own dedicated kernel thread.

questions.question: What is a drawback of the One-to-One multithreading model?
options: It causes the whole process to block easily
Creating a user thread creates a kernel thread, causing overhead
questions.correctAnswer: Creating a user thread creates a kernel thread, causing overhead
questions.explanation: In the One-to-One model, creating a user thread requires creating a corresponding kernel thread, which adds overhead and can limit the total number of threads.

questions.question: Which multithreading model allows developers to create as many user threads as necessary without restricting concurrency on multiprocessors?
questions.explanation: The Many-to-Many model multiplexes many user-level threads onto a smaller or equal number of kernel threads, allowing flexible thread creation and true multiprocessor execution.

questions.question: What provides the programmer with an API for creating and managing threads?
questions.explanation: A Thread Library provides programmers with an API for creating and managing threads.

questions.question: A thread library implemented entirely in user space invokes library functions as:
options: Local function calls in user space
questions.correctAnswer: Local function calls in user space
questions.explanation: A user-space thread library has all code and data structures in user space, so invoking a library function results in a local function call rather than a system call.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the three primary thread libraries in use today?
questions.explanation: The three main thread libraries highlighted in the lecture are POSIX Pthreads, Windows threads, and Java threads.

questions.question: Java threads are managed by:
questions.explanation: Java threads are managed by the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) and typically implemented using the thread model provided by the underlying host OS.

questions.question: What is the standard practice for creating a thread in Java?
questions.explanation: While a class can extend Thread, the standard practice in Java is implementing the Runnable interface.

questions.question: In Java, which method must be overridden when implementing the Runnable interface?
questions.explanation: Implementing the Runnable interface requires defining and overriding the run() method.

questions.question: In a Java thread, what method is used to cause the main thread to wait until a worker thread finishes?
questions.explanation: Calling join() on a worker thread makes the calling thread wait until that worker thread finishes execution.

questions.question: What happens if the `join()` method is NOT used in the Java example when printing a computed result?
options: The output is not guaranteed and might print the uninitialized value
questions.correctAnswer: The output is not guaranteed and might print the uninitialized value
questions.explanation: Without join(), the main thread may read and print the shared result variable before the worker thread finishes computing it.

questions.question: Which OS natively provides a kernel-level thread library?
questions.explanation: The Windows thread library is a kernel-level library available directly on Windows systems.

questions.question: A Kernel thread is sometimes called a:
questions.explanation: The lecture notes that a kernel thread is also referred to as a Lightweight Process (LWP).

questions.question: Distributing threads across cores where each thread performs a unique operation is known as:
questions.explanation: Task parallelism distributes threads across cores so that each thread executes a unique operation.

questions.question: A traditional process has a single thread of control.
questions.explanation: A traditional (heavyweight) process has a single thread of control, whereas multithreaded processes have multiple threads of control.

questions.question: Concurrency requires a multicore architecture to function.
questions.explanation: Concurrency can occur on a single processor core via time-slicing scheduler switches; parallelism is what requires multiple cores.

questions.question: Kernel threads are generally more expensive to create than user threads.
questions.explanation: Kernel threads are supported and managed directly by the OS kernel, making them slower and more expensive to create and manage than user-level threads.

questions.question: In the Many-to-One model, multiple threads can run in parallel on a multicore system.
questions.explanation: Because all user threads map to a single kernel thread in the Many-to-One model, only one thread can access the kernel at a time, preventing parallel execution on multicore systems.

questions.question: Java threads are available on any system that provides a JVM.
questions.explanation: Because Java threads are managed by the JVM, they are available on any host platform that provides a JVM.
